title: White Fang
author: London, Jack
paragraph_text: But at front and rear, unawed and indomitable, toiled the two men who were not yet dead. Their bodies were covered with fur and soft-tanned leather. Eyelashes and cheeks and lips were so coated with the crystals from their frozen breath that their faces were not discernible. This gave them the seeming of ghostly masques, undertakers in a spectral world at the funeral of some ghost. But under it all they were men, penetrating the land of desolation and mockery and silence, puny adventurers bent on colossal adventure, pitting themselves against the might of a world as remote and alien and pulseless as the abysses of space.
reasoning: Q1: Author's tone is detectably admiring/reverent toward the men — the passage elevates them against an indifferent, crushing landscape. Canonical vocabulary fits cleanly: 'admiring,' 'reverent,' 'earnest.' Q2: Tone toward the subject (the men vs. the wilderness) is dominant; atmospheric description is in service of the tonal signal rather than competing with it as a separate primitive. Q3: Fully self-contained. 'Puny adventurers bent on colossal adventure' is an overt internal contrast that signals admiring irony — the smallness of the men is acknowledged but their drive is celebrated. No external schema required; the Yukon wilderness context is established within the passage through 'desolation,' 'mockery,' 'silence,' 'alien,' 'pulseless.' Q4: Syntax is complex but manageable; the long closing sentence builds in a way that reinforces the tonal signal rather than obscuring it. Vocabulary density is elevated but resolvable from context. The 'ghostly masques/funeral' imagery is one figurative cluster that could add mild load but does not block the dominant tonal signal. Q5: 5a — at least 3 discrete target-supporting elements ('puny adventurers bent on colossal adventure,' 'unawed and indomitable,' 'pitting themselves against the might of a world...as the abysses of space') plus 2-3 non-supporting descriptive elements (fur/leather clothing, frozen breath details, ghostly masques simile). 5c — dominant concept is 'admiring' or 'reverent' with strong distractors available: 'sympathetic' (wrong register — too passive), 'detached' (wrong — author is invested), 'solemn' (partial — misses the celebratory elevation). 5d — craft pivot identifiable at 'But under it all they were men' — London explicitly breaks from the ghostly/spectral frame to assert human identity and drive, a nameable structural move.

title: White Fang
author: London, Jack
paragraph_text: After a searching scrutiny, the animal trotted forward a few steps. This it repeated several times, till it was a short hundred yards away. It paused, head up, close by a clump of spruce trees, and with sight and scent studied the outfit of the watching men. It looked at them in a strangely wistful way, after the manner of a dog; but in its wistfulness there was none of the dog affection. It was a wistfulness bred of hunger, as cruel as its own fangs, as merciless as the frost itself.
reasoning: Q1: Author's tone is detectable — London deliberately corrects a sentimental reading (dog-like wistfulness = affection) by redefining wistfulness as hunger-driven cruelty, signaling a sympathetic-but-unsentimental, even sobering authorial stance toward the animal. The canonical term 'unsentimental' approximates 'earnest' or 'sobering'; 'detached' and 'sympathetic' are both in play, making the tone genuinely nameable. Q2: The dominant cognitive work is identifying what the author is doing with the corrective pivot — not plot, not character emotion, not symbolism requiring outside knowledge. Q3: Fully self-contained. The pivot ('but in its wistfulness there was none of the dog affection') is explicit on the page; a student can read the redefinition without any schema. The wolf-dog wilderness context is universally accessible. Q4: Vocabulary is within range for Title I 9th grade with sentence context support ('scrutiny,' 'wistfulness,' 'merciless' are resolvable). No cognitive overload. Q5: 5a supported — target-supporting elements (the corrective redefinition, the hunger-cruelty equation) contrast clearly with neutral behavioral description (trotting, pausing, studying). 5c supported — dominant concept is author correcting sentimental misreading toward an earnest/unsentimental stance; 'wistful,' 'sympathetic,' 'mocking,' and 'detached' are plausible distractors with genuine discriminability.

title: White Fang
author: London, Jack
paragraph_text: With night came horror. Not only were the starving wolves growing bolder, but lack of sleep was telling upon Henry. He dozed despite himself, crouching by the fire, the blankets about his shoulders, the axe between his knees, and on either side a dog pressing close against him. He awoke once and saw in front of him, not a dozen feet away, a big grey wolf, one of the largest of the pack. And even as he looked, the brute deliberately stretched himself after the manner of a lazy dog, yawning full in his face and looking upon him with a possessive eye, as if, in truth, he were merely a delayed meal that was soon to be eaten.
reasoning: The author's tone is clearly sympathetic toward Henry and darkly ironic/grim toward the predatory situation — the wolf's casual, almost contemptuous ease ('yawning full in his face,' 'merely a delayed meal') reveals London's sardonic, unsentimental attitude toward nature's indifference to human survival. This is detectable entirely from word choice on the page: 'possessive eye,' 'delayed meal,' 'brute,' and the wolf's lazy-dog demeanor applied to a lethal predator all signal an ironic, grimly amused authorial voice. No external schema required. The dominant signal is tone/authorial attitude, not character emotion or plot action per se. 5a works: 2-3 target-supporting phrases (the wolf's possessive gaze, 'delayed meal,' the yawning) contrast clearly with neutral descriptive elements (Henry's blankets, the fire, the axe). 5c works: 'ironic' or 'grimly sardonic' is the dominant nameable concept with plausible distractors (sympathetic, suspenseful, detached). Clean isolation — vocabulary is accessible, figurative language is self-explanatory.

title: My Ántonia
author: Cather, Willa
paragraph_text: We went all the way in day-coaches, becoming more sticky and grimy with each stage of the journey. Jake bought everything the newsboys offered him: candy, oranges, brass collar buttons, a watch-charm, and for me a ‘Life of Jesse James,’ which I remember as one of the most satisfactory books I have ever read. Beyond Chicago we were under the protection of a friendly passenger conductor, who knew all about the country to which we were going and gave us a great deal of advice in exchange for our confidence. He seemed to us an experienced and worldly man who had been almost everywhere; in his conversation he threw out lightly the names of distant states and cities. He wore the rings and pins and badges of different fraternal orders to which he belonged. Even his cuff-buttons were engraved with hieroglyphics, and he was more inscribed than an Egyptian obelisk.
reasoning: The author's tone toward the conductor is gently amused and ironic — presenting him as pompous and self-important through the accumulation of badges, rings, engraved cuff-buttons, and the obelisk comparison — while the child narrator's perspective ('seemed to us an experienced and worldly man') is earnest and admiring. The target skill here is precisely the gap between what the narrator believes and what Cather signals through ironic diction and comic overload. The obelisk simile is the craft pivot for 5d. A student can be asked to name the author's attitude (amused/ironic) vs. the narrator's attitude (admiring), distinguishing the two. No external schema is required: the humor of a train conductor covered in fraternal badges being compared to an Egyptian monument is self-contained. The Jesse James reference and grimy coach details serve as clean non-supporting foils. 5c is strongly supported: the dominant signal is 'amused' or 'ironic,' with plausible distractors of 'admiring' (narrator's surface tone), 'critical' (too harsh), and 'sympathetic' (misreading the warmth). 5a passes with 3+ discrete pointable elements at different signal levels.

title: My Ántonia
author: Cather, Willa
paragraph_text: I do not remember crossing the Missouri River, or anything about the long day’s journey through Nebraska. Probably by that time I had crossed so many rivers that I was dull to them. The only thing very noticeable about Nebraska was that it was still, all day long, Nebraska.
reasoning: The passage carries a clean, detectable wry/ironic tone toward Nebraska as a subject. The author's attitude — amused dismissal, dry understatement — is readable from the words on the page alone: 'dull to them' signals deliberate underreaction, and the recursive tautology 'Nebraska was still, all day long, Nebraska' is a self-contained comic construction requiring no external schema. A Title I 9th grader can detect the joke without knowing anything about Cather, the novel, or the period. Q1 passes: the tone is nameable (amused, ironic, wry — canonical terms apply). Q2 passes: the dominant work is tone-reading, not plot or character emotion. Q3 passes: the ironic mechanism lives entirely in the words — the tautology is self-explanatory, 'dull to them' is accessible diction. Q4 passes: short, clean, no syntax barriers. Q5: 5a is constructable — at least 2 target-supporting elements (tautology line, 'dull to them') vs. 2 neutral/surface-descriptive elements ('long day's journey,' 'crossing the Missouri River'); 5c is constructable — dominant tone is amused/ironic with plausible distractors (nostalgic, detached, wistful, solemn); 5d is constructable — the tautological sentence structure ('Nebraska was still, all day long, Nebraska') is an identifiable craft device at a named location students can point to.

title: My Ántonia
author: Cather, Willa
paragraph_text: The minute supper was over, Otto took me into the kitchen to whisper to me about a pony down in the barn that had been bought for me at a sale; he had been riding him to find out whether he had any bad tricks, but he was a ‘perfect gentleman,’ and his name was Dude. Fuchs told me everything I wanted to know: how he had lost his ear in a Wyoming blizzard when he was a stage-driver, and how to throw a lasso. He promised to rope a steer for me before sundown next day. He got out his ‘chaps’ and silver spurs to show them to Jake and me, and his best cowboy boots, with tops stitched in bold design—roses, and true-lover’s knots, and undraped female figures. These, he solemnly explained, were angels.
reasoning: The passage carries a clearly amused, affectionate tone. The dominant authorial signal is gentle amusement at Fuchs's earnest, unselfconscious machismo — culminating in the punchline that naked female figures on his boots were 'solemnly explained' to be angels. The word 'solemnly' applied to this absurd explanation is the sharpest tone signal: the author is amused, not mocking cruelly, not reverent. A 9th grader can detect this from words on the page alone — the incongruity between 'undraped female figures' and 'angels,' underlined by 'solemnly,' is self-contained irony requiring no external schema. The rest of the passage (pony purchase, lasso tricks, lost ear) provides non-supporting neutral/descriptive foil elements. Q5 passes on 5a (3-4 discrete pointable elements at different signal levels) and 5c (clean dominant tone — 'amused' or 'affectionate' — with tempting distractors: 'reverent,' 'admiring,' 'wistful'). No harmful language present. No schema dependency. Format is prose memoir/fiction narration — source context flags first-person but this reads as novelistic narration of childhood memory and functions as prose fiction for assessment purposes.

title: My Ántonia
author: Cather, Willa
paragraph_text: The oldest son, Ambroz—they called it Ambrosch—came out of the cave and stood beside his mother. He was nineteen years old, short and broad-backed, with a close-cropped, flat head, and a wide, flat face. His hazel eyes were little and shrewd, like his mother’s, but more sly and suspicious; they fairly snapped at the food. The family had been living on corncakes and sorghum molasses for three days.
reasoning: The author's tone is detectably critical and somewhat contemptuous toward Ambroz — 'sly and suspicious,' 'fairly snapped at the food,' and the reductive physical description ('flat head,' 'wide, flat face') all carry a distancing, unflattering authorial attitude. These are words on the page requiring no period schema or external knowledge. The final sentence about corncakes and sorghum molasses for three days introduces a complicating sympathetic note, which creates useful discrimination: a student must distinguish the author's critical/contemptuous characterization of Ambroz from the sympathetic framing of the family's poverty — a clean tone_misreading instructional opportunity. The dominant tone toward the character (contemptuous/critical) is separable from the pathos of circumstances, making 5a and 5c viable. The passage is self-contained, vocabulary is accessible in context, and no external schema is required. No harmful language triggers. Note: the physical description language is reductive/clinical in Cather's period style but does not rise to historically harmful ethnic language requiring rejection.

title: Leaves of Grass
author: Whitman, Walt
paragraph_text: Here, take this gift, I was reserving it for some hero, speaker, or general, One who should serve the good old cause, the great idea, the progress and freedom of the race, Some brave confronter of despots, some daring rebel; But I see that what I was reserving belongs to you just as much as to any.
reasoning: The passage carries a clear earnest/affectionate tone: the speaker elevates the ordinary reader to the level of hero, rebel, and general through a deliberate pivot on 'But I see.' The tone is detectably earnest and tender — the author's attitude toward the reader (reverent, democratizing, admiring) is readable purely from the words on the page. The initial catalog of grand figures functions as a foil that makes the final democratic turn legible without any external schema — students understand the social weight of 'hero' and 'rebel' universally. The pivot word 'But' is a clean structural signal. No schema-gating: 'despots' and 'rebel' are self-contextualizing. The passage is short, syntactically manageable, and not verse in the sense of dense lyric compression — it reads as a direct address. For 5a, supporting elements (the catalog of heroes, the pivot) contrast clearly against neutral/surface elements (the gift framing, the abstract cause language). For 5c, 'earnest' or 'affectionate' is dominant and three plausible distractors (solemn, nostalgic, critical) are genuinely tempting and wrong. Q5 passes on 5a and 5c.

title: Leaves of Grass
author: Whitman, Walt
paragraph_text: The man’s body is sacred and the woman’s body is sacred, No matter who it is, it is sacred--is it the meanest one in the laborers’ gang? Is it one of the dull-faced immigrants just landed on the wharf? Each belongs here or anywhere just as much as the well-off, just as much as you, Each has his or her place in the procession.
reasoning: Whitman's tone is earnest and reverent — the dominant signal is the author's sincere, unironic affirmation of universal human dignity. The word 'sacred' is repeated with explicit emphasis, and the rhetorical questions about laborers and immigrants serve as foils that a student might misread as critical or dismissive (the phrase 'dull-faced' could be mistaken as contemptuous), creating a productive distractor for tone_misreading intervention. The author's attitude is consistently admiring/reverent toward the marginalized subjects, not mocking or pitying. No external schema is required: 'laborers,' 'immigrants,' and 'well-off' are universally accessible social categories. Vocabulary is period-flavored but self-contained. 5a works because 'dull-faced immigrants' and 'meanest one in the laborers' gang' are surface-level non-flattering descriptors that could mislead a student into reading the tone as critical or contemptuous, while the 'sacred' repetitions and 'each belongs here' clearly signal reverence. 5c works cleanly: 'reverent' is the dominant nameable concept with strong distractors (contemptuous, pitying, critical) available from the passage itself.

title: Leaves of Grass
author: Whitman, Walt
paragraph_text: Do you know so much yourself that you call the meanest ignorant? Do you suppose you have a right to a good sight, and he or she has no right to a sight? Do you think matter has cohered together from its diffuse float, and the soil is on the surface, and water runs and vegetation sprouts, For you only, and not for him and her?
reasoning: The passage is a sequence of rhetorical questions directed at a presumptuous, self-centered reader, with Whitman's author attitude being earnestly indignant and morally challenging — not the reader's mood, not a character's emotion. The tone signal is carried entirely by word choice and sentence structure on the page: the repeated 'Do you' challenges, the contrast between 'you' and 'him and her,' and the closing rhetorical twist about nature belonging to all. No historical schema, allusions, or institutional knowledge required. A Title I 9th grader can identify that the author is indignant and disapproving of the assumption of superiority purely from the challenge structure. For Q5: 5a passes — clear supporting elements (the rhetorical challenges) vs. non-supporting elements (the nature description sentences); 5c passes — dominant tone is 'indignant' or 'earnest' with tempting distractors like 'admiring,' 'wistful,' or 'solemn'; 5d passes — the repeated anaphoric rhetorical question structure ('Do you...Do you suppose...Do you think') is a nameable craft feature. The passage is short but sufficiently dense for 5a given the strong contrast between the accusatory questions and the neutral descriptive nature imagery.

title: Leaves of Grass
author: Whitman, Walt
paragraph_text: If any thing is sacred the human body is sacred, And the glory and sweet of a man is the token of manhood untainted, And in man or woman a clean, strong, firm-fibred body, is more beautiful than the most beautiful face.
reasoning: The author's tone is reverent and earnest toward the human body — signaled by 'sacred' (used twice for emphasis), 'glory,' and the superlative claim that a strong body surpasses even the most beautiful face. These word choices are self-contained and require no external schema; a 9th grader can read the elevation language directly. The tone signal is dominant and unambiguous. Q4 is manageable despite archaic phrasing ('firm-fibred,' 'token of manhood untainted') because context resolves meaning. For 5a, target-supporting elements ('sacred,' 'glory,' 'more beautiful than the most beautiful face') contrast with neutral/descriptive elements ('in man or woman,' 'the most beautiful face') to build a usable discrimination item. For 5c, 'reverent' is clearly dominant and three plausible distractors — admiring (partially correct but shallower), solemn, earnest — create genuine discrimination challenge. Verse format noted but prose-like syntax and lack of line breaks reduces verse rejection trigger; passage reads as elevated prose. Format exclusion for verse applies most cleanly to lineated poetry; this excerpt presents as continuous prose in context.

title: The Country of the Pointed Firs
author: Jewett, Sarah Orne
paragraph_text: He rose with dignity to take leave, and asked me to stop at his house some day, when he would show me some outlandish things that he had brought home from sea. I was familiar with the subject of the decadence of shipping interests in all its affecting branches, having been already some time in Dunnet, and I felt sure that Captain Littlepage's mind had now returned to a safe level.
reasoning: The narrator's tone is amused and gently condescending toward Captain Littlepage. The irony is accessible from the words alone: 'familiar with the subject... in all its affecting branches' signals weary over-exposure rather than genuine interest, and 'returned to a safe level' implies the narrator had been quietly judging the captain's mental stability throughout — a dismissive but understated judgment delivered with dry humor. No external schema required: the irony operates through diction ('affecting,' 'safe level') and the narrator's self-presentation as a patient sufferer of the captain's obsessions. A Title I 9th grader can detect 'amused' or 'condescending' from the words on the page. 5a works because there are 2 clear target-supporting phrases and 2 neutral/character-action phrases. 5c works because 'amused' or 'wry/condescending' is the dominant signal with plausible distractors of 'sympathetic,' 'admiring,' or 'solemn.'

title: The Country of the Pointed Firs
author: Jewett, Sarah Orne
paragraph_text: I heard her going down into the cool little cellar, and then there was considerable delay. When she returned, mug in hand, I noticed the taste of camomile, in spite of my protest; but its flavor was disguised by some other herb that I did not know, and she stood over me until I drank it all and said that I liked it.
reasoning: The author's tone toward the herbalist character is affectionate and amused — the narrator submits to being dosed with a remedy she protested, then forced to declare she liked it. This is gently ironic and warmly comic, not bitter or critical. The tone signal is carried entirely by words on the page: 'in spite of my protest,' 'disguised,' 'stood over me until I drank it all and said that I liked it.' No external schema required — the social dynamic of an elder figure insisting a reluctant recipient take medicine and then approve of it is universally legible. The skill work is distinguishing the author's amused affection from the character's mild annoyance. Q5 passes 5a: supporting elements (protest ignored, flavor disguised, forced approval) contrast cleanly against neutral descriptive elements (cellar, delay, mug in hand). Passes 5c: 'amused' or 'affectionate' is the dominant nameable tone with plausible distractors including 'sympathetic,' 'disapproving,' or 'wistful.'

title: The Country of the Pointed Firs
author: Jewett, Sarah Orne
paragraph_text: I had become well acquainted with Mrs. Todd as landlady, herb-gatherer, and rustic philosopher; we had been discreet fellow-passengers once or twice when I had sailed up the coast to a larger town than Dunnet Landing to do some shopping; but I was yet to become acquainted with her as a mariner. An hour later we pushed off from the landing in the desired dory. The tide was just on the turn, beginning to fall, and several friends and acquaintances stood along the side of the dilapidated wharf and cheered us by their words and evident interest. Johnny Bowden and I were both rowing in haste to get out where we could catch the breeze and put up the small sail which lay clumsily furled along the gunwale. Mrs. Todd sat aft, a stern and unbending lawgiver.
reasoning: The passage carries a clearly detectable affectionate and amused tone toward Mrs. Todd. The author's word choices — 'rustic philosopher,' 'stern and unbending lawgiver,' and the gentle humor of cataloguing her roles (landlady, herb-gatherer, philosopher, mariner) — signal an author who finds her subject charming and gently funny rather than merely describing her. The comic incongruity of calling Mrs. Todd a 'lawgiver' while she sits in a small dory on a coastal errand is self-contained irony accessible from words on the page alone. No external schema is required — a 9th grader can recognize the gap between the grand title and the humble setting. Q2 dominance holds because the tone signal is the primary cognitive work; the plot action (pushing off, rowing) is thin and subordinate. Q4 is clean — vocabulary like 'dory,' 'gunwale,' and 'aft' is period-flavored but resolvable from context (they're in a small boat). For 5a, target-supporting elements ('stern and unbending lawgiver,' 'rustic philosopher') contrast clearly with neutral nautical/action details. For 5c, 'affectionate' or 'amused' is the dominant nameable concept with plausible distractors: 'admiring' (too straight), 'detached' (narrator is present but not cold), 'solemn' (surface reading of 'stern').

title: The Country of the Pointed Firs
author: Jewett, Sarah Orne
paragraph_text: When we caught the wind we were soon on our seaward course, and only stopped to underrun a trawl, for the floats of which Mrs. Todd looked earnestly, explaining that her mother might not be prepared for three extra to dinner; it was her brother's trawl, and she meant to just run her eye along for the right sort of a little haddock. I leaned over the boat's side with great interest and excitement, while she skillfully handled the long line of hooks, and made scornful remarks upon worthless, bait-consuming creatures of the sea as she reviewed them and left them on the trawl or shook them off into the waves. At last we came to what she pronounced a proper haddock, and having taken him on board and ended his life resolutely, we went our way.
reasoning: The passage carries an affectionate, amused authorial tone toward Mrs. Todd — the narrator's word choices ('scornful remarks upon worthless, bait-consuming creatures,' 'ended his life resolutely,' 'she pronounced a proper haddock') render Mrs. Todd's unsentimental pragmatism with clear warmth and gentle humor. The author is not mocking Mrs. Todd but is clearly charmed by her. This tone is readable entirely from words on the page: 'scornful' and 'worthless' applied to fish, the bureaucratic gravity of 'pronounced a proper haddock,' and the matter-of-fact 'ended his life resolutely' all signal amusement and affection without requiring period knowledge, institutional schema, or literary allusion. Period vocabulary ('trawl,' 'haddock') is resolvable from context — fishing activity is self-evident. The dominant cognitive work is tone detection, not plot parsing. At least 3-4 discrete pointable evidence elements support 5a; the clean dominant signal (affectionate/amused) with plausible distractors (admiring, sympathetic, detached) supports 5c.

title: The Scarlet Letter
author: Hawthorne, Nathaniel
paragraph_text: It may be, however,—O, transporting and triumphant thought!—that the great-grandchildren of the present race may sometimes think kindly of the scribbler of bygone days, when the antiquary of days to come, among the sites memorable in the town’s history, shall point out the locality of THE TOWN PUMP!
reasoning: The passage is self-contained and readable without external schema. The tone signal is ironic/amused self-deprecation: the author mock-elevates a mundane town pump to the status of a historic landmark, using theatrical exclamation ('O, transporting and triumphant thought!') and capitalizing 'THE TOWN PUMP' as if it were a monument, while calling himself a mere 'scribbler.' The absurdity of imagining future antiquarians reverently pointing out a water pump is detectable from words on the page alone — no period knowledge required. The irony mechanism operates through contrast between grandiose framing ('triumphant,' 'memorable,' 'locality') and the trivial subject (a pump). Q3 passes: a Title I 9th grader can feel the mismatch between the solemn ceremonial language and the mundane referent. For Q5: 5a passes — 'O, transporting and triumphant thought!' and 'THE TOWN PUMP!' are clearly irony-supporting; 'the great-grandchildren of the present race may sometimes think kindly' and 'among the sites memorable in the town's history' surface as apparently sincere and serve as foils. 5c passes — dominant tone is ironic/amused with plausible distractors (earnest, nostalgic, wistful). 5d passes — the capitalization of 'THE TOWN PUMP' is an identifiable craft feature at a specific nameable location that a teacher can point to as carrying the ironic punch.

title: The Scarlet Letter
author: Hawthorne, Nathaniel
paragraph_text: The voice which had called her attention was that of the reverend and famous John Wilson, the eldest clergyman of Boston, a great scholar, like most of his contemporaries in the profession, and withal a man of kind and genial spirit. This last attribute, however, had been less carefully developed than his intellectual gifts, and was, in truth, rather a matter of shame than self-congratulation with him. There he stood, with a border of grizzled locks beneath his skull-cap; while his gray eyes, accustomed to the shaded light of his study, were winking, like those of Hester’s infant, in the unadulterated sunshine. He looked like the darkly engraved portraits which we see prefixed to old volumes of sermons; and had no more right than one of those portraits would have, to step forth, as he now did, and meddle with a question of human guilt, passion, and anguish.
reasoning: The passage opens with surface-level praise ('reverend and famous,' 'great scholar,' 'kind and genial spirit') that Hawthorne immediately undercuts with his own editorial commentary — 'less carefully developed,' 'a matter of shame,' and the devastating final clause about having 'no more right' to meddle. The author's contemptuous/critical attitude toward Wilson is the dominant signal and operates entirely through word choice and authorial intrusion visible on the page. No schema is required: the ironic pivot from flattery to undercutting is accessible to a 9th grader via universal social understanding of how praise followed by 'but' or 'however' works. The infant-blinking simile further diminishes Wilson by comparing him to a helpless newborn. The final sentence is a clean, quotable craft pivot (5d) where Hawthorne steps in as narrator to render judgment. Canonical vocabulary 'contemptuous' or 'critical' fits clearly; 'admiring' or 'reverent' serve as strong distractors (surface-level positive descriptors in the opening). Q4 is borderline due to some archaic diction ('withal,' 'prefixed'), but sentence context resolves both, and the dominant ironic mechanism is syntactically accessible. Passes 5a, 5c, and 5d.

title: The Scarlet Letter
author: Hawthorne, Nathaniel
paragraph_text: The vulgar, who, in those dreary old times, were always contributing a grotesque horror to what interested their imaginations, had a story about the scarlet letter which we might readily work up into a terrific legend. They averred, that the symbol was not mere scarlet cloth, tinged in an earthly dye-pot, but was red-hot with infernal fire, and could be seen glowing all alight, whenever Hester Prynne walked abroad in the night-time. And we must needs say, it seared Hester’s bosom so deeply, that perhaps there was more truth in the rumor than our modern incredulity may be inclined to admit.
reasoning: The author's tone is detached and skeptical-yet-earnest in a distinctive split register: he dismisses the 'vulgar' crowd's superstition with mild condescension ('grotesque horror,' 'terrific legend'), yet pivots to semi-sincerely entertain the rumor's symbolic truth ('perhaps there was more truth in the rumor'). This creates a readable ironic-yet-sympathetic authorial stance students can detect from word choice alone — 'vulgar,' 'we might readily work up,' and 'our modern incredulity' all signal the author positioning himself above superstition while winking at its metaphorical validity. No schema dependencies: the scarlet letter is named and contextualized within the passage, the folk story is self-explanatory, and the ironic pivot is carried entirely by the words on the page. Q4 is borderline given archaic vocabulary ('averred,' 'infernal,' 'incredulity'), but sentence context makes meanings recoverable. For 5a, target-supporting evidence ('vulgar,' 'readily work up into a terrific legend,' 'perhaps there was more truth') contrasts clearly with non-supporting narrative content (the folk description of glowing letter, Hester walking at night). For 5c, 'skeptical' or 'ironic' is a dominant nameable concept with 'sympathetic,' 'earnest,' and 'critical' as plausible distractors. Passage passes.

title: The Scarlet Letter
author: Hawthorne, Nathaniel
paragraph_text: On the wall hung a row of portraits, representing the forefathers of the Bellingham lineage, some with armor on their breasts, and others with stately ruffs and robes of peace. All were characterized by the sternness and severity which old portraits so invariably put on; as if they were the ghosts, rather than the pictures, of departed worthies, and were gazing with harsh and intolerant criticism at the pursuits and enjoyments of living men.
reasoning: The passage carries a clear ironic/mocking tone toward the portraits and by extension the puritanical ancestors they represent. Hawthorne's authorial attitude — wry contempt for the judgmental severity of these forebears — is detectable entirely from word choice on the page: 'harsh and intolerant criticism,' 'ghosts,' 'invariably,' and the ironic label 'departed worthies' all signal the author's dismissive amusement without requiring any knowledge of The Scarlet Letter's plot, Puritan history, or period institutions. The word 'worthies' functions as readable irony from context alone (the portraits are severe and harsh, hardly worthy of admiration). title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
author: Douglass, Frederick
paragraph_text: There were no beds given the slaves, unless one coarse blanket be considered such, and none but the men and women had these. This, however, is not considered a very great privation. They find less difficulty from the want of beds, than from the want of time to sleep; for when their day’s work in the field is done, the most of them having their washing, mending, and cooking to do, and having few or none of the ordinary facilities for doing either of these, very many of their sleeping hours are consumed in preparing for the field the coming day; and when this is done, old and young, male and female, married and single, drop down side by side, on one common bed,—the cold, damp floor,—each covering himself or herself with their miserable blankets; and here they sleep till they are summoned to the field by the driver’s horn. At the sound of this, all must rise, and be off to the field. There must be no halting; every one must be at his or her post; and woe betides them who hear not this morning summons to the field; for if they are not awakened by the sense of hearing, they are by the sense of feeling: no age nor sex finds any favor. Mr. Severe, the overseer, used to stand by the door of the quarter, armed with a large hickory stick and heavy cowskin, ready to whip any one who was so unfortunate as not to hear, or, from any other cause, was prevented from being ready to start for the field at the sound of the horn.

title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave

paragraph_text: The home plantation of Colonel Lloyd wore the appearance of a country village. All the mechanical operations for all the farms were performed here. The shoemaking and mending, the blacksmithing, cartwrighting, coopering, weaving, and grain-grinding, were all performed by the slaves on the home plantation. The whole place wore a business-like aspect very unlike the neighboring farms. The number of houses, too, conspired to give it advantage over the neighboring farms. It was called by the slaves the _Great House Farm._ Few privileges were esteemed higher, by the slaves of the out-farms, than that of being selected to do errands at the Great House Farm. It was associated in their minds with greatness. A representative could not be prouder of his election to a seat in the American Congress, than a slave on one of the out-farms would be of his election to do errands at the Great House Farm. They regarded it as evidence of great confidence reposed in them by their overseers; and it was on this account, as well as a constant desire to be out of the field from under the driver’s lash, that they esteemed it a high privilege, one worth careful living for. He was called the smartest and most trusty fellow, who had this honor conferred upon him the most frequently. I have often sung to drown my sorrow, but seldom to express my happiness. Crying for joy, and singing for joy, were alike uncommon to me while in the jaws of slavery. title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave

paragraph_text: Colonel Lloyd kept a large and finely cultivated garden, which afforded almost constant employment for four men, besides the chief gardener, (Mr. M’Durmond.) This garden was probably the greatest attraction of the place. During the summer months, people came from far and near—from Baltimore, Easton, and Annapolis—to see it. It abounded in fruits of almost every description, from the hardy apple of the north to the delicate orange of the south. This garden was not the least source of trouble on the plantation. Its excellent fruit was quite a temptation to the hungry swarms of boys, as well as the older slaves, belonging to the colonel, few of whom had the virtue or the vice to resist it. Scarcely a day passed, during the summer, but that some slave had to take the lash for stealing fruit. The colonel had to resort to all kinds of stratagems to keep his slaves out of the garden. The last and most successful one was that of tarring his fence all around; after which, if a slave was caught with any tar upon his person, it was deemed sufficient proof that he had either been into the garden, or had tried to get in. In either case, he was severely whipped by the chief gardener. This plan worked well; the slaves became as fearful of tar as of the lash. title: My Bondage and My Freedom

paragraph_text: The name of this singularly unpromising and truly famine stricken district is Tuckahoe, a name well known to all Marylanders, black and white. It was given to this section of country probably, at the first, merely in derision; or it may possibly have been applied to it, as I have heard, because some one of its earlier inhabitants had been guilty of the petty meanness of stealing a hoe—or taking a hoe that did not belong to him. Eastern Shore men usually pronounce the word _took_, as _tuck; Took-a-hoe_, therefore, is, in Maryland parlance, _Tuckahoe_. But, whatever may have been its origin—and about this I will not be positive—that name has stuck to the district in question; and it is seldom mentioned but with contempt and derision, on account of the barrenness of its soil, and the ignorance, indolence, and poverty of its people. title: My Bondage and My Freedom
author: Douglass, Frederick
paragraph_text: The reader will pardon so much about the place of my birth, on the score that it is always a fact of some importance to know where a man is born, if, indeed, it be important to know anything about him. In regard to the _time_ of my birth, I cannot be as definite as I have been respecting the _place_. Nor, indeed, can I impart much knowledge concerning my parents. Genealogical trees do not flourish among slaves. A person of some consequence here in the north, sometimes designated _father_, is literally abolished in slave law and slave practice. It is only once in a while that an exception is found to this statement. I never met with a slave who could tell me how old he was. Few slave-mothers know anything of the months of the year, nor of the days of the month. They keep no family records, with marriages, births, and deaths. They measure the ages of their children by spring time, winter time, harvest time, planting time, and the like; but these soon become undistinguishable and forgotten. Like other slaves, I cannot tell how old I am. This destitution was among my earliest troubles. I learned when I grew up, that my master—and this is the case with masters generally—allowed no questions to be put to him, by which a slave might learn his age. Such questions deemed evidence of impatience, and even of impudent curiosity. From certain events, however, the dates of which I have since learned, I suppose myself to have been born about the year 1817.

title: My Bondage and My Freedom
author: Douglass, Frederick
paragraph_text: Grandmother pointed out my brother PERRY, my sister SARAH, and my sister ELIZA, who stood in the group. I had never seen my brother nor my sisters before; and, though I had sometimes heard of them, and felt a curious interest in them, I really did not understand what they were to me, or I to them. We were brothers and sisters, but what of that? Why should they be attached to me, or I to them? Brothers and sisters we were by blood; but _slavery_ had made us strangers. I heard the words brother and sisters, and knew they must mean something; but slavery had robbed these terms of their true meaning. The experience through which I was passing, they had passed through before. They had already been initiated into the mysteries of old master’s domicile, and they seemed to look upon me with a certain degree of compassion; but my heart clave to my grandmother. Think it not strange, dear reader, that so little sympathy of feeling existed between us. The conditions of brotherly and sisterly feeling were wanting—we had never nestled and played together. My poor mother, like many other slave-women, had many _children_, but NO FAMILY! The domestic hearth, with its holy lessons and precious endearments, is abolished in the case of a slave-mother and her children. “Little children, love one another,” are words seldom heard in a slave cabin.

title: My Bondage and My Freedom
author: Douglass, Frederick
paragraph_text: Summoned away to her account, with the impassable gulf of slavery between us during her entire illness, my mother died without leaving me a single intimation of _who_ my father was. There was a whisper, that my master was my father; yet it was only a whisper, and I cannot say that I ever gave it credence. Indeed, I now have reason to think he was not; nevertheless, the fact remains, in all its glaring odiousness, that, by the laws of slavery, children, in all cases, are reduced to the condition of their mothers. This arrangement admits of the greatest license to brutal slaveholders, and their profligate sons, brothers, relations and friends, and gives to the pleasure of sin, the additional attraction of profit. title: Up from Slavery: An Autobiography

paragraph_text: It has been my fortune to meet personally many of what are called great characters, both in Europe and America, but I do not hesitate to say that I never met any man who, in my estimation, was the equal of General Armstrong. Fresh from the degrading influences of the slave plantation and the coal-mines, it was a rare privilege for me to be permitted to come into direct contact with such a character as General Armstrong. I shall always remember that the first time I went into his presence he made the impression upon me of being a perfect man: I was made to feel that there was something about him that was superhuman. It was my privilege to know the General personally from the time I entered Hampton till he died, and the more I saw of him the greater he grew in my estimation. One might have removed from Hampton all the buildings, class-rooms, teachers, and industries, and given the men and women there the opportunity of coming into daily contact with General Armstrong, and that alone would have been a liberal education. The older I grow, the more I am convinced that there is no education which one can get from books and costly apparatus that is equal to that which can be gotten from contact with great men and women. Instead of studying books so constantly, how I wish that our schools and colleges might learn to study men and things!

paragraph_text: It would be difficult to describe the hold that he had upon the students at Hampton, or the faith they had in him. In fact, he was worshipped by his students. It never occurred to me that General Armstrong could fail in anything that he undertook. There is almost no request that he could have made that would not have been complied with. When he was a guest at my home in Alabama, and was so badly paralyzed that he had to be wheeled about in an invalid’s chair, I recall that one of the General’s former students had occasion to push his chair up a long, steep hill that taxed his strength to the utmost. When the top of the hill was reached, the former pupil, with a glow of happiness on his face, exclaimed, “I am so glad that I have been permitted to do something that was real hard for the General before he dies!” While I was a student at Hampton, the dormitories became so crowded that it was impossible to find room for all who wanted to be admitted. title: Up from Slavery: An Autobiography

paragraph_text: In some way, however, I had gotten hold of an extra, second-hand coat which I thought was a pretty valuable coat. This I decided to sell, in order to get a little money for travelling expenses. I had a good deal of boyish pride, and I tried to hide, as far as I could, from the other students the fact that I had no money and nowhere to go. I made it known to a few people in the town of Hampton that I had this coat to sell, and, after a good deal of persuading, one coloured man promised to come to my room to look the coat over and consider the matter of buying it. This cheered my drooping spirits considerably. Early the next morning my prospective customer appeared. After looking the garment over carefully, he asked me how much I wanted for it. I told him I thought it was worth three dollars. He seemed to agree with me as to price, but remarked in the most matter-of-fact way: “I tell you what I will do; I will take the coat, and will pay you five cents, cash down, and pay you the rest of the money just as soon as I can get it.” It is not hard to imagine what my feelings were at the time.

title: Up from Slavery: An Autobiography
author: Washington, Booker T.
paragraph_text: Naturally, most of our people who received some little education became teachers or preachers. While among those two classes there were many capable, earnest, godly men and women, still a large proportion took up teaching or preaching as an easy way to make a living. Many became teachers who could do little more than write their names. I remember there came into our neighbourhood one of this class, who was in search of a school to teach, and the question arose while he was there as to the shape of the earth and how he could teach the children concerning the subject. title: Frederick Douglass

paragraph_text: The next meeting of importance was in Buffalo. The outlook for a convention in this western New York city was so discouraging that Mr. Douglass’s associates turned on their heels and left him to “do Buffalo alone.” The place appointed was a dilapidated old room that had once been used as a post-office. No one was there at first except a few hack-drivers who sauntered in from curiosity. But Mr. Douglass went at them with great earnestness, as if they could settle all the problems that were overburdening his heart. Out of this small and unsympathetic beginning, grew a great convention. Every day for nearly a week, in the old building, he spoke to constantly increasing crowds of people who were worth talking to, until finally a large Baptist church was thrown open to him. Here the size and character of the audience were flattering. So great was the eagerness to hear him that on Sunday evening he addressed an outdoor meeting of five thousand people in the park.

title: Frederick Douglass

paragraph_text: The contrast between the conditions of his coming to England and those of his returning to the United States affords an interesting evidence of his power of conquest. title: Frederick Douglass
author: Washington, Booker T.
paragraph_text: In Boston an attempt was made to “silence” him. Stones were thrown in the meeting at Norristown, Pa., and at a very large assembly held in the court house at Harrisburg, Pa., on the 9th of August, 1847, after Mr. Garrison had spoken without molestation, Douglass was violently interrupted when he tried to speak, and was not allowed to continue. But such disturbances were not general, nor did they have the effect of shaking the eloquent apostle’s determination to be heard. During the same month he and Garrison held numerous anti-slavery meetings in Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, and Ohio. There was in these meetings abundant evidence that the cause of Abolition was gaining ground. The gatherings in Oberlin and Cleveland were especially notable for the interest manifested. One of the Cleveland papers had the following notice of the meeting: “The Menagerie Company, Garrison, Douglass, Foster (and we expect Satan) are to be here on Saturday next and open at seven o’ clock in the evening in the big tent, and continue their harangues over the Sabbath. title: Frederick Douglass

paragraph_text: Various reasons were given for this attitude. Mr. Garrison thought it quite “impractical to combine the editor and the lecturer without either causing the paper to be more or less neglected, or the sphere of lecturing to be seriously circumscribed.” It was further urged that the publication was not needed, that it would diminish the support of the papers already in existence, and that it could not succeed. Some of Douglass’s other friends advised him, that being a man without any education and without any literary training, he would make himself ridiculous as an editor. These counselors wished to save him from the humiliation of an ignominious failure, and cautioned him against the mistake of allowing his ambition to bring him into ridicule and contempt. This opposition coming from his former advisers and associates caused him to hesitate, and, for a time, to give up the scheme; so, instead of starting the paper as soon as he received the money to be devoted to that purpose, he postponed the project for nearly a year, out of deference to the judgment of these wise and close friends.

title: Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl, Written by Herself
author: Jacobs, Harriet A. (Harriet Ann)
paragraph_text: After repeated quarrels between the doctor and his wife, he announced his intention to take his youngest daughter, then four years old, to sleep in his apartment. It was necessary that a servant should sleep in the same room, to be on hand if the child stirred. I was selected for that office, and informed for what purpose that arrangement had been made. By managing to keep within sight of people, as much as possible, during the day time, I had hitherto succeeded in eluding my master, though a razor was often held to my throat to force me to change this line of policy. At night I slept by the side of my great aunt, where I felt safe. He was too prudent to come into her room. She was an old woman, and had been in the family many years. Moreover, as a married man, and a professional man, he deemed it necessary to save appearances in some degree. But he resolved to remove the obstacle in the way of his scheme; and he thought he had planned it so that he should evade suspicion. He was well aware how much I prized my refuge by the side of my old aunt, and he determined to dispossess me of it. The first night the doctor had the little child in his room alone. The next morning, I was ordered to take my station as nurse the following night. A kind Providence interposed in my favor. During the day Mrs. Flint heard of this new arrangement, and a storm followed. I rejoiced to hear it rage.

title: Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl, Written by Herself
author: Jacobs, Harriet A. (Harriet Ann)
paragraph_text: I did as she ordered. As I went on with my account her color changed frequently, she wept, and sometimes groaned. She spoke in tones so sad, that I was touched by her grief. The tears came to my eyes; but I was soon convinced that her emotions arose from anger and wounded pride. She felt that her marriage vows were desecrated, her dignity insulted; but she had no compassion for the poor victim of her husband’s perfidy. She pitied herself as a martyr; but she was incapable of feeling for the condition of shame and misery in which her unfortunate, helpless slave was placed. Yet perhaps she had some touch of feeling for me; for when the conference was ended, she spoke kindly, and promised to protect me. I should have been much comforted by this assurance if I could have had confidence in it; but my experiences in slavery had filled me with distrust. She was not a very refined woman, and had not much control over her passions. I was an object of her jealousy, and, consequently, of her hatred; and I knew I could not expect kindness or confidence from her under the circumstances in which I was placed. I could not blame her. Slaveholders’ wives feel as other women would under similar circumstances. The fire of her temper kindled from small sparks, and now the flame became so intense that the doctor was obliged to give up his intended arrangement.
reasoning: The passage carries a clearly dominant authorial tone that is simultaneously critical and sympathetic — critical toward the mistress's self-pity and incapacity for empathy, sympathetic toward the narrator's helpless condition. The author's attitude is distinct from the character emotions (the mistress weeping, the narrator feeling touched), making this a clean tone_misreading target. The irony in 'I could not blame her' and the pivot 'but she had no compassion' signal authorial stance without requiring external schema. Slavery is named and contextualized within the passage; no institutional or historical foreknowledge is required to read the tone. The mistress's tears and the promise of kindness serve as strong non-supporting distractors (surface-level sympathy) against the author's underlying critical/indignant stance. 5a is strongly supported: at least 2 target-supporting quotables and 2 non-supporting foils. 5c is supported: the dominant tone is 'indignant' or 'critical' with tempting distractors of 'sympathetic' (surface reading of narrator's tears) or 'bitter.' No format exclusions triggered; first-person memoir is contextually appropriate for tone_misreading. No harmful language flags.

title: Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl, Written by Herself
author: Jacobs, Harriet A. (Harriet Ann)
paragraph_text: My mistress grew weary of her vigils; they did not prove satisfactory. She changed her tactics. She now tried the trick of accusing my master of crime, in my presence, and gave my name as the author of the accusation. To my utter astonishment, he replied, “I don’t believe it; but if she did acknowledge it, you tortured her into exposing me.” Tortured into exposing him! Truly, Satan had no difficulty in distinguishing the color of his soul! I understood his object in making this false representation. It was to show me that I gained nothing by seeking the protection of my mistress; that the power was still all in his own hands. I pitied Mrs. Flint. She was a second wife, many years the junior of her husband; and the hoary-headed miscreant was enough to try the patience of a wiser and better woman. She was completely foiled, and knew not how to proceed. She would gladly have had me flogged for my supposed false oath; but, as I have already stated, the doctor never allowed any one to whip me. The old sinner was politic. The application of the lash might have led to remarks that would have exposed him in the eyes of his children and grandchildren. How often did I rejoice that I lived in a town where all the inhabitants knew each other! If I had been on a remote plantation, or lost among the multitude of a crowded city, I should not be a living woman at this day.

The author also expresses guarded sympathy toward Mrs. Flint ('I pitied Mrs. Flint'), creating a tonal contrast that supports discrimination items. The indignant authorial voice — distinct from the narrator-as-character's fear — is the dominant signal throughout. No schema-gated allusions: 'Satan' functions as universal moral reference, not a Biblical allusion requiring doctrinal knowledge. 'Hoary-headed' may be unfamiliar but is resolvable from the age context. Q4 is clean: vocabulary is period-flavored but sentence context anchors meaning. Supports 5a (pointable target vs. non-supporting evidence elements) and 5c (bitter/contemptuous as dominant nameable tone with plausible distractors: sympathetic, detached, nostalgic, wistful). title: Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl, Written by Herself
author: Jacobs, Harriet A. (Harriet Ann)
paragraph_text: Reader, I draw no imaginary pictures of southern homes. I am telling you the plain truth. Yet when victims make their escape from this wild beast of Slavery, northerners consent to act the part of bloodhounds, and hunt the poor fugitive back into his den, “full of dead men’s bones, and all uncleanness.” Nay, more, they are not only willing, but proud, to give their daughters in marriage to slaveholders. The poor girls have romantic notions of a sunny clime, and of the flowering vines that all the year round shade a happy home. To what disappointments are they destined! The young wife soon learns that the husband in whose hands she has placed her happiness pays no regard to his marriage vows. Children of every shade of complexion play with her own fair babies, and too well she knows that they are born unto him of his own household. Jealousy and hatred enter the flowery home, and it is ravaged of its loveliness.

At least 3-4 discrete pointable supporting elements exist for 5a. The passage also has strong cross-text pairing potential with other abolitionist or slave narrative excerpts (5e flag). title: The Red Record: Tabulated Statistics and Alleged Causes of Lynching in the United States
author: Wells-Barnett, Ida B.
paragraph_text: The only excuse which capital punishment attempts to find is upon the theory that the criminal is past the power of reformation and his life is a constant menace to the community. If, however, he is mentally unbalanced, irresponsible for his acts, there can be no more inhuman act conceived of than the wilful sacrifice of his life. So thoroughly is that principle grounded in the law, that all civilized society surrounds human life with a safeguard, which prevents the execution of a criminal who is insane, even if sane at the time of his criminal act. Should he become insane after its commission the law steps in and protects him during the period of his insanity. But Lynch Law has no such regard for human life. Assuming for itself an absolute supremacy over the law of the land, it has time and again dyed its hands in the blood of men who were imbeciles. Two or three noteworthy cases will suffice to show with what inhuman ferocity irresponsible men have been put to death by this system of injustice.

No schema-gated knowledge is required; the passage itself defines Lynch Law, contrasts it with formal legal protections, and provides its own context. The contrast structure (law protects the insane / Lynch Law does not) makes the indignant tone readable to a Title I 9th grader without external knowledge of specific institutions beyond what is named and explained internally. title: The Red Record: Tabulated Statistics and Alleged Causes of Lynching in the United States
author: Wells-Barnett, Ida B.
paragraph_text: One would suspect that the civilization which defends itself against the barbarisms of Lynch Law by stating that it lynches human beings only when they are guilty of awful attacks upon women and children, would have been very careful to have given these four prisoners, who were simply charged with arson, a fair trial, to which they were entitled upon every principle of law and humanity. Especially would this seem to be the case when if is considered that one of the prisoners charged was a woman, and if the nineteenth century has shown any advancement upon any lines of human action, it is preeminently shown in its reverence, respect and protection of its womanhood. But the people of Alabama failed to have any regard for womanhood whatever.

title: The Red Record: Tabulated Statistics and Alleged Causes of Lynching in the United States
author: Wells-Barnett, Ida B.
paragraph_text: No class of American citizens stands in greater need of the humane and thoughtful consideration of all sections of our country than do the colored people, nor does any class exceed us in the measure of grateful regard for acts of kindly interest in our behalf. It is, therefore, to us, a matter of keen regret that a Christian organization, so large and influential as the Woman's Christian Temperance Union, should refuse to give its sympathy and support to our oppressed people who ask no further favor than the promotion of public sentiment which shall guarantee to every person accused of crime the safeguard of a fair and impartial trial, and protection from butchery by brutal mobs. Accustomed as we are to the indifference and apathy of Christian people, we would bear this instance of ill fortune in silence, had not Miss Willard gone out of her way to antagonize the cause so dear to our hearts by including in her Annual Address to the W.C.T.U. Convention at Cleveland, November 5, 1894, a studied, unjust and wholly unwarranted attack upon our work.

title: The Red Record: Tabulated Statistics and Alleged Causes of Lynching in the United States
author: Wells-Barnett, Ida B.
paragraph_text: This paragraph, brief as it is, contains two statements which have not the slightest foundation in fact. At no time, nor in any place, have I made statements "concerning white women having taken the initiative in nameless acts between the races." Further, at no time, or place nor under any circumstance, have I directly or inferentially "put an imputation upon half the white race in this country" and I challenge this "friend and well-wisher" to give proof of the truth of her charge. Miss Willard protests against lynching in one paragraph and then, in the next, deliberately misrepresents my position in order that she may criticise a movement, whose only purpose is to protect our oppressed race from vindictive slander and Lynch Law.

title: Southern Horrors: Lynch Law in All Its Phases
author: Wells-Barnett, Ida B.
paragraph_text: This cry has had its effect. It has closed the heart, stifled the conscience, warped the judgment and hushed the voice of press and pulpit on the subject of lynch law throughout this "land of liberty." Men who stand high in the esteem of the public for Christian character, for moral and physical courage, for devotion to the principles of equal and exact justice to all, and for great sagacity, stand as cowards who fear to open their mouths before this great outrage. They do not see that by their tacit encouragement, their silent acquiescence, the black shadow of lawlessness in the form of lynch law is spreading its wings over the whole country.

title: Southern Horrors: Lynch Law in All Its Phases
author: Wells-Barnett, Ida B.
paragraph_text: When Barrett came he led a _posse_ of officers, twelve in number, who afterward claimed to be hunting a man for whom they had a warrant. That twelve men in citizen's clothes should think it necessary to go in the night to hunt one man who had never before been arrested, or made any record as a criminal has never been explained. When they entered the back door the young men thought the threatened attack was on, and fired into them. Three of the officers were wounded, and when the _defending_ party found it was officers of the law upon whom they had fired, they ceased and got away.

The italicized 'defending' reframes the shooters as victims, not aggressors — a pointed authorial choice. title: Southern Horrors: Lynch Law in All Its Phases
author: Wells-Barnett, Ida B.
paragraph_text: The Afro-Americans of Memphis denounced the lynching of three of their best citizens, and urged and waited for the authorities to act in the matter and bring the lynchers to justice. No attempt was made to do so, and the black men left the city by thousands, bringing about great stagnation in every branch of business. Those who remained so injured the business of the street car company by staying off the cars, that the superintendent, manager and treasurer called personally on the editor of the _Free Speech_, asked them to urge our people to give them their patronage again. Other business men became alarmed over the situation and the _Free Speech_ was run away that the colored people might be more easily controlled. A meeting of white citizens in June, three months after the lynching, passed resolutions for the first time, condemning it. _But they did not punish the lynchers._ Every one of them was known by name, because they had been selected to do the dirty work, by some of the very citizens who passed these resolutions. Memphis is fast losing her black population, who proclaim as they go that there is no protection for the life and property of any Afro-American citizen in Memphis who is not a slave.
reasoning: Q1: The passage carries a strong, nameable tone — indignant and bitter — detectable through word choice ('dirty work,' 'no protection...who is not a slave'), italicized emphasis ('But they did not punish the lynchers'), and the ironic juxtaposition of resolutions condemning lynching passed by men who organized it. Q2: Tone is the dominant signal; the narrative facts serve as vehicles for the author's attitude rather than as plot or character work. Q3: Fully self-contained. The passage defines the lynching, the civic inaction, the economic boycott, and the hypocrisy of the resolutions — no external schema required. title: The call of the wild
author: London, Jack
paragraph_text: He swiftly lost the fastidiousness which had characterized his old life. A dainty eater, he found that his mates, finishing first, robbed him of his unfinished ration. There was no defending it. While he was fighting off two or three, it was disappearing down the throats of the others. To remedy this, he ate as fast as they; and, so greatly did hunger compel him, he was not above taking what did not belong to him. He watched and learned. When he saw Pike, one of the new dogs, a clever malingerer and thief, slyly steal a slice of bacon when Perrault’s back was turned, he duplicated the performance the following day, getting away with the whole chunk. A great uproar was raised, but he was unsuspected; while Dub, an awkward blunderer who was always getting caught, was punished for Buck’s misdeed.
reasoning: The passage carries an admiring — even subtly amused — tone toward Buck's rapid moral adaptation. London's word choices signal authorial attitude clearly: 'fastidiousness' marks the old life with mild irony; 'he was not above taking what did not belong to him' frames theft with understated approval; 'duplicated the performance' treats theft as skillful mimicry; and the final image of Dub punished for Buck's crime is presented with detached satisfaction rather than moral alarm. The author's attitude is distinctly sympathetic-to-admiring, separate from any character emotion or plot suspense. No schema is required — the tone signal lives entirely in diction and what London chooses to frame approvingly. For 5a, target-supporting elements (the 'fastidiousness' pivot, 'not above taking,' 'duplicated the performance,' Dub punished) contrast cleanly with neutral plot-action elements (fighting off dogs, watching Pike). For 5c, 'admiring' is the dominant nameable tone with strong distractors in 'sympathetic,' 'critical,' and 'amused.' Vocabulary density is manageable for a Title I 9th grader with sentence-context support ('fastidiousness,' 'malingerer' can be decoded from surrounding context). No harmful language detected. Clean pass on all five criteria.

title: The call of the wild
author: London, Jack
paragraph_text: This first theft marked Buck as fit to survive in the hostile Northland environment. It marked his adaptability, his capacity to adjust himself to changing conditions, the lack of which would have meant swift and terrible death. It marked, further, the decay or going to pieces of his moral nature, a vain thing and a handicap in the ruthless struggle for existence. It was all well enough in the Southland, under the law of love and fellowship, to respect private property and personal feelings; but in the Northland, under the law of club and fang, whoso took such things into account was a fool, and in so far as he observed them he would fail to prosper.

It marked') that actually scaffolds reading rather than impeding it. Vocabulary is period-flavored but resolvable in context. The author's attitude is neither mourning nor celebrating moral decay — he frames it as simply rational, which is the core cynical/detached move students must identify.

title: The call of the wild
author: London, Jack
paragraph_text: Not that Buck reasoned it out. He was fit, that was all, and unconsciously he accommodated himself to the new mode of life. All his days, no matter what the odds, he had never run from a fight. But the club of the man in the red sweater had beaten into him a more fundamental and primitive code. Civilized, he could have died for a moral consideration, say the defence of Judge Miller’s riding-whip; but the completeness of his decivilization was now evidenced by his ability to flee from the defence of a moral consideration and so save his hide. He did not steal for joy of it, but because of the clamor of his stomach. He did not rob openly, but stole secretly and cunningly, out of respect for club and fang. In short, the things he did were done because it was easier to do them than not to do them.
reasoning: Q1: The tone signal is clearly sympathetic-to-admiring, with a tinge of wistfulness — London presents Buck's moral degradation not with contempt but with clinical admiration, framing survival pragmatism as a kind of completeness. The canonical terms sympathetic and wistful (or earnest) are nameable from words on the page. Q2: Tone is the dominant signal; plot action (Buck stealing, fleeing) is present but subordinate — the passage is structured as authorial commentary on Buck's transformation, not as action narration. 'Judge Miller's riding-whip' contextualizes Buck's former life adequately without requiring prior novel knowledge — the contrast between 'dying for a moral consideration' over a riding whip versus pragmatic survival is readable as ironic juxtaposition from context alone. 'Decivilization' is a coined word whose meaning is compositionally transparent. No schema-gated allusions. Q4: Syntax is manageable; one or two harder constructions ('the completeness of his decivilization was now evidenced by') but resolvable in context. No heavy figurative overlay blocking access. Q5: 5a — clear target-supporting vs. non-supporting element split available. 5c — dominant tone is sympathetic/admiring with earnest narration; plausible distractors include contemptuous, critical, indignant, mocking — genuinely tempting misreads. 5d — structural pivot between 'Civilized, he could have died' and 'the completeness of his decivilization' is a nameable diction and structural contrast point. 5e flagged: strong pairing candidate for passages treating animal or human survival pragmatism with authorial sympathy vs. moral judgment (e.g., Naturalist or Social Darwinist framing).

title: The call of the wild
author: London, Jack
paragraph_text: Perrault took a hand. Between them they ran him about for the better part of an hour. They threw clubs at him. He dodged. They cursed him, and his fathers and mothers before him, and all his seed to come after him down to the remotest generation, and every hair on his body and drop of blood in his veins; and he answered curse with snarl and kept out of their reach. He did not try to run away, but retreated around and around the camp, advertising plainly that when his desire was met, he would come in and be good.
reasoning: The author's tone is distinctly amused — London treats the humans' increasingly absurd, escalating cursing ('every hair on his body and drop of blood in his veins') with comic exaggeration, and frames the dog's behavior with wry anthropomorphism ('advertising plainly... he would come in and be good'), making the dog's negotiating logic sound almost rational while the humans look ridiculous. This is author attitude (amused, affectionate toward the dog) clearly separable from character emotion (the humans are furious). A Title I 9th grader can detect this from word choice alone: the hyperbolic curse list signals mockery of the humans, while 'advertising plainly' signals the author's affectionate amusement at the dog. No schema dependency. The curse escalation and 'advertising plainly' clause are the two clearest target-supporting evidence anchors for 5a discrimination, and the dominant tone of 'amused' is clean enough for 5c with plausible distractors (sympathetic, admiring, critical).

title: White Fang
author: London, Jack
paragraph_text: In advance of the dogs, on wide snowshoes, toiled a man. At the rear of the sled toiled a second man. On the sled, in the box, lay a third man whose toil was over,—a man whom the Wild had conquered and beaten down until he would never move nor struggle again. It is not the way of the Wild to like movement. Life is an offence to it, for life is movement; and the Wild aims always to destroy movement. It freezes the water to prevent it running to the sea; it drives the sap out of the trees till they are frozen to their mighty hearts; and most ferociously and terribly of all does the Wild harry and crush into submission man—man who is the most restless of life, ever in revolt against the dictum that all movement must in the end come to the cessation of movement.

The canonical terms 'solemn,' 'indignant,' and 'earnest' all apply, with 'solemn' and 'earnest' being most dominant. Words like 'ferociously,' 'harry,' 'crush,' 'offence,' and 'destroy' carry the author's attitude without any cultural or historical prerequisite.
